en: Every living beast and creature
Stirred and raced across the ground.
The people woke and the camp grew restless,
Expecting an order from the commander;
The whole host stood waiting.
And there, behold Chyngtengir,
Clad in his robe of blue steel,
Raging like a blue-gray tiger.
Suurultai, resourceful in counsel,
Was an extraordinarily mighty khan,
And he had countless
Cunning judges of men.
Those who always traveled with him,
Those of surpassing wisdom,
Eloquent masters of speech—
He gathered many from the people.
The keen-eyed among them,
The sages who had seen much,
The judges who unraveled knots—
He roused them all together
And left none behind.
Men who would strike with an ax when challenged,
Men who could conceive far-reaching counsel,
The narrow men of wicked thought,
Craftsmen fit for every task,
Men who had cast aside weakness and proved their valor,
Steady, watchful champions—
Chyngtengir gathered them without exception,
Then raised his voice and began to speak,
Speaking quietly but with force:
Zhelzhetpes, who goes between the sides—
No soul can pass where Zhelzhetpes cannot.
Let Zhetpes go as the intermediary;
Let him carry word throughout the world.
Let him take six pack mules,
Let him take ample provisions,
Warriors who can drink and never sate on blood,
Who spare no life once battle begins.
Whose single head, if demanded,
Could be staked against a multitude—
Let him take such champion warriors beside him.
Let him travel the four corners
Of this round world in four circuits,
And through all five corners of the earth
Pass marking what he sees.
Let him find a mountain to strike,
Let him find an enemy to fight,
Let him find a man to face him.
Who dwell in Ala-Too,
Whose six forefathers were khans,
Who answer to no one in the world,
Who multiply whenever they are slain,
Whom holy Khizr himself follows—
The Kyrgyz race of sovereign will—
Let Zhelzhetpes go and take their measure.
Tell them to submit
To my decree and to my word;
Tell them to give their treasure and their daughter
As tribute to Lord Tengir.
If they will not heed my word,
If they do not gather their herds and people
And offer them before me as tribute,
If they refuse to declare submission
And do not bow their heads,
Let them gird themselves for battle,
And come to the ground of slaughter;
Let none of those Kyrgyz remain behind,
To the field where we shall grind one another down!
They say the Kyrgyz have a Kenen,
That his myriad troops stand ready,
That he is a hero surpassing all the world.
Kermekash is the loveliest of maidens;
Tell him to surrender Kermekash.
And, living on undying and undimmed,
There is the peerless courser Kertulpar—
To sovereign Chyngtengir
Tell him to present both of them!
If he will not heed these words,
If that whoreson Kenen
Will give neither horse nor daughter,
I shall set fire to his farthest bounds;
If he draws my wrath,
I shall crush him and take his head!
If my rage truly seizes me,
If he will not obey what I have said,
Will not submit in truth and bow his head,
Will not come as my subject,
I shall not let him turn his plow,
Nor turn his hand to earning a living!
I shall not let him tread the face of the earth,
Nor scatter any seed for grain;
I shall allow him no livelihood at all!
If my full rage comes upon me,
I shall slaughter his countless myriads,
Send them wandering like the yellow plague,
And visit them with an incurable affliction!
Firing upon them from every ridge,
I shall wipe out every last one!
Tell him to submit to these words
And pay tribute to Lord Khan!
Go, Zhelzhetpes, go;
Go to those swaggering Kyrgyz,
Whose every weapon stands ready,
From Kenen, the giant of the Kyrgyz,
Go and bring back word.
Travel without tiring on your journey;
Return five days from now,
Late by no more than a mare's milking.
Sharpen your tongue and speak without fear.
The tribute and spoil I have named—
The radiant girl with gazelle eyes,
The beauty I desire,
The tempest with reins of hair,
The one who truly sets the heart aflame—
Drive back that prize without fail!
Complete the mission on which I send you;
Prepare and bring everything I have named!
So saying, Chyngtengir
Named fortunate Zholkerchik
And gave him to Zhetpes as a companion.
One who devoured all he encountered,
Zholbors, he also gave to Zhetpes.
To travel among the people
And learn the people's condition,
He took six pack mules,
Put on a coat no bullet could pierce,
And took twelve mighty champions.
Readied like a lion,
He set out toward Ala-Too;
Zhelzhetpes took to the road.
Ask no more about Zhelzhetpes:
White and pure within, corrupt without,
No other such soul has lived in an age.
They called him a son come from the Kyrgyz,
Half Kyrgyz and half Chinese,
A go-between for the peoples of two tribes,
A man of two divided minds.
He was the goldsmith of the Chinese,
The one who loaded gold upon mules,
The one who drew out men's secrets,
A diviner who observed and discerned,
Then laughed without speaking openly.
Unable to know whether he was Kyrgyz,
Unable to recognize his Chineseness,
He went about muttering to himself.
When Zhelzhetpes heard this, he thought:
— Every wish I had has come true;
I have been given all I desired.
My failing enterprise has turned aright,
My flown bird has come home to perch.
Swiftly invoking Baabedin,
He rode out on his embassy,
To go among the people.
Then Zhelzhetpes said:
“We shall keep going on patrol;
Sooner or later we shall learn
How great his fury is.
Let us survey the land,
Let us scout the far side of the ridge.
We shall speak misleading words,
Avoiding battle with the white-capped people,
Binding the army and leading it astray,
Guiding the host by another road,
Gathering up its surging ranks;
We shall drive this hellish infidel
Against the mountains and the rocks,
Turn his army into a flock of blind sheep,
Lead them the wrong way,
And set them on a false road.
Somehow we must save
The offspring of the brave Kyrgyz,
The descendants of the valiant wolves.
Let us pray for the people’s safety;
Say there is escape in flight,
And, if we can, shepherd the people away.
If we do not carry out this ruse,
No pleading will save us
From this cruel, mighty swine.
He destroys anyone who stirs;
He makes wretched women and young children weep,
With no fear of the sin.”
Having said this, Zhelzhetpes
Told it to those who would go,
And firmly instructed the envoys.
Clad in a loose, drooping coat,
Mounted on a long-striding mule,
He set out on a journey of many days,
Crossing passes and roaming deserts,
Enduring great hardship;
Thus Zhelzhetpes went on his way.
He crossed rough, humped passes,
And followed many winding roads,
Saw rivers and deserts,
Saw the lands of many tribes;
Day waned and night passed,
His poor life nearly spent,
Yet where would a hero ever shrink back?
He reached the Ala-Too.
When he looked upon the Ala-Too,
It held every kind of adorned treasure,
And foxes in countless hosts;
There were deer in its sheltered places,
Ibex on its crags,
Snow upon its mountains,
Game within its forests;
There were lions and wild boars,
Bears and tigers as well;
It had sorrel grass for fermenting mare’s milk,
And an abundance of every wealth.
It was a land inhabited by heroes,
A people living free and at ease.
Zhelzhetpes saw all this.
“If that furious swine attacks,
Where will their villages settle?
What recourse will they have?” he thought.
Seeing their blue-green pastures and rocky cliffs,
Their thoroughbreds and swift steeds mingled together,
He grieved at the sight of their herds.
All radiant and crimson,
He grieved at the sight of their lives.
Before he could send word to the people,
The wise Ebegei and Kogoi,
With their twin sons in their train,
Had ranged an immense distance.
Taking Alymsaryk and Kulansaryk,
The two heroes, as companions,
They had gone on a great hunt,
Hunting lions and pursuing tigers.
The two giants, Ebegei and Kogoi,
Were both beside themselves.
Earlier they had dreamed a dream,
Foretelling calamity upon their heads;
They had sensed a threat to their tiny lives,
And dreamed on behalf of the true Kyrgyz.
Ebegei and Kogoi summoned
The twin tigers, born of one lair,
The two lion-like champions.
When the two arrived,
Ebegei spoke softly and began his tale,
Laying great weight upon its ending.
He came forth into the daylight:
“My sons, interpret the dream I saw.”
Then brave Kogoi began to speak:
“My two tigers, born of one lair,
In my sleep I saw a grievous dream,
And saw calamity upon calamity:
Blood covered the Ala-Too,
Dust covered the plain below;
The people cried out, the nation was in turmoil,
And all was steeped in black blood.”
The vast herds, the people, and all their wealth
Lay helpless, finding no way out.
“My son, what can this mean?
When brave Kogoi dreamed at night,
Fire swept in from the sunrise,
